common_name: Stapleford Gem Penstemon (Bicolor Mauve-and-Pink Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Stapleford Gem is a long-grown English hybrid border penstemon and RHS Award of Garden Merit holder, valued for its bicolor mauve-and-pink flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; good drainage through winter matters more than summer moisture for this borderline-hardy hybrid. Stapleford Gem bears tall, branching spikes of tubular flowers in soft mauve and pink shades over a white throat boldly striped with maroon, blooming heavily from midsummer into early autumn and drawing bees steadily throughout. It combines the vigor and free-flowering habit typical of the classic English hybrid border penstemons with an unusually soft, blended flower color that sets it apart from the more solid-colored cultivars in the group. In colder parts of its range, leave the old top growth in place over winter as frost protection and cut back hard in spring once new growth appears at the base; avoid heavy, waterlogged soil, which the crown does not tolerate.

common_name: Chester Scarlet Penstemon (Bright Crimson-Scarlet Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Chester Scarlet is a classic English hybrid border penstemon grown for its large, bright crimson-scarlet flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; sharp winter drainage is essential, since this hybrid is more likely to be lost to a wet crown than to cold alone. Chester Scarlet produces erect, branching spikes of large, narrowly bell-shaped, bright crimson-scarlet flowers lightly marked white in the throat, blooming heavily from summer into early autumn on a robust, upright plant with broad, glossy leaves. Its saturated hot color makes it one of the showiest reds among the English hybrid border penstemons, and it draws bees and, in North American gardens, hummingbirds throughout its long bloom season. In cold areas apply a dry winter mulch and leave old stems standing until spring, then cut back hard once new basal growth appears.

common_name: Maurice Gibbs Penstemon (Wine-Red Bicolor Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Maurice Gibbs is an English hybrid border penstemon noted for its bright wine-red to cerise flowers with a contrasting white throat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; good drainage through winter is the main factor in this hybrid's survival, since it tolerates summer heat and dry spells without difficulty. Maurice Gibbs bears loose, branching spikes of tubular flowers in a vivid wine-red to cerise shade with a sharply contrasting white mouth and throat, blooming continuously from midsummer into early autumn on a bushy, well-branched plant. The hot, saturated flower color reads strongly from a distance and pairs well with the softer pastels of other border penstemon cultivars, and bees work the flowers steadily throughout the season. In colder areas, leave old growth in place as winter protection and cut back hard in spring, and avoid heavy, waterlogged soil that encourages crown rot.

common_name: Alice Hindley Penstemon (Tall Lilac-Blue Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Alice Hindley is a tall, RHS Award of Garden Merit-winning English hybrid border penstemon with soft lilac-blue flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; this hybrid is among the taller border penstemons and benefits from some shelter from strong wind as well as sharp winter drainage. Alice Hindley bears tall, willowy spikes of large tubular flowers in mauve suffused with soft lilac and pale pink, opening to a white throat, blooming from midsummer well into autumn on a vigorous, upright plant. Its height and soft, blended coloring make it a standout at the back of a mixed perennial border, and bees and, in North American gardens, hummingbirds visit the long-lasting flowers steadily. Leave old growth standing over winter as frost protection in cold areas, cut back hard once new basal shoots appear in spring, and avoid rich, waterlogged soil that encourages crown rot.

common_name: Countess of Dalkeith Penstemon (Royal Purple Bicolor Hybrid Beardtongue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Countess of Dalkeith is a long-cultivated English hybrid border penstemon with rich royal purple flowers and a bold white throat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; sharp winter drainage matters more than soil fertility for this borderline-hardy hybrid. Countess of Dalkeith bears upright stems of tubular flowers in rich royal purple with a bold, sharply contrasting white throat, blooming from midsummer into early autumn with the free-flowering habit typical of the classic English hybrid border penstemons. The strong purple-and-white contrast makes it a striking companion for the softer pinks and mauves of other border penstemon cultivars, and bees visit the flowers heavily throughout the season. In cold areas, apply a dry winter mulch and leave old stems in place until spring, then cut back hard once new growth resumes at the base; avoid heavy, waterlogged soil, which shortens the plant's life.

common_name: Desert Sunrise Agastache (Sunset-Colored Hybrid Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Transplant out after the danger of frost in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Desert Sunrise is a High Country Gardens hybrid of Agastache rupestris and Agastache cana bred for a long, non-stop bloom season and sunset-toned flowers.

directions: Plant in lean to average, sharply drained soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, since this hybrid is far more prone to winter crown rot in wet soil than to any problem from summer heat or drought. Desert Sunrise bears dense spikes of tubular flowers that blend orange, pink, and lavender like a sunrise on the horizon, over aromatic, mint-scented gray-green foliage, blooming non-stop from midsummer through fall. It combines the xeric toughness of Agastache rupestris with the adaptability to regular garden soil and moisture inherited from Agastache cana, and it is an exceptional hummingbird plant that also draws bees throughout its long season. Cut back old flowering stems in late winter just before new growth resumes, and avoid rich soil or heavy winter mulch piled against the crown, both of which encourage rot.
